subject: Medicine
topic: Hereditary Hemochromatosis Diagnostic Algorithm and Therapeutic Phlebotomy
stem: A 52-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 9-month history of worsening fatigue, loss of energy, and generalized joint stiffness. The joint pain primarily involves his bilateral second and third metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, wrists, and knees, with morning stiffness lasting approximately 20 minutes. He also reports a gradual decrease in libido and new erectile dysfunction over the past year. He drinks one glass of wine on weekends and takes no medications. Family history is notable for a brother who developed cirrhosis of unknown etiology in his 50s. Physical examination reveals subtle grayish-slate hyperpigmentation over the face, neck, and dorsum of the hands. Musculoskeletal exam demonstrates bony swelling and mild tenderness to palpation of the second and third MCP joints bilaterally, without warm synovial effusion. Abdominal examination reveals a firm, non-tender liver edge palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin. Neurological and genital examinations demonstrate decreased testicular volume bilaterally. Laboratory evaluation: fasting serum glucose 162 mg/dL, serum AST 68 U/L, ALT 74 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, and total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL. Fasting serum iron is 210 mcg/dL, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) is 260 mcg/dL (transferrin saturation 81%; normal 20-50%), and serum ferritin is 1,650 ng/mL (normal 30-300 ng/mL). Which of the following represents the most appropriate next step to establish the definitive diagnosis and direct disease-modifying treatment?

options.text: Diagnostic liver biopsy to evaluate for Mallory-Denk bodies and initiate oral penicillamine chelation therapy
options.explanation: Mallory-Denk bodies and penicillamine copper chelation are features of Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), not hereditary hemochromatosis; Wilson disease features low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings.

options.text: Initiation of daily oral deferasirox iron chelation therapy and avoidance of phlebotomy due to risk of hemodynamic collapse
options.explanation: Therapeutic phlebotomy is the undisputed first-line treatment for hereditary hemochromatosis; oral iron chelators (deferasirox, deferoxamine) are reserved only for secondary iron overload (e.g., thalassemia major, sickle cell disease) with severe chronic anemia where phlebotomy is impossible.

options.text: Prescription of high-dose oral methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine for suspected rheumatoid arthritis
options.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis typically involves symmetric PIP and MCP synovitis with prolonged morning stiffness (> 1 hour) and inflammatory autoantibodies (RF, anti-CCP); it does not cause transferrin saturation of 81%, bronze skin, or hypogonadism.

options.text: Genetic testing for HFE gene mutations (C282Y and H63D) and initiation of weekly therapeutic phlebotomy targeting serum ferritin between 50 and 100 ng/mL
options.explanation: HEREDITARY HEMOCHROMATOSIS (HH) is an autosomal recessive disorder of iron metabolism most commonly caused by mutations in the HFE gene on chromosome 6 (primarily C282Y homozygosity or C282Y/H63D compound heterozygosity). PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Mutated HFE impairs hepatic sensing of iron stores, causing inappropriate suppression of the iron-regulatory hormone HEPCIDIN. Low hepcidin leads to uncontrolled, excessive basolateral ferroportin export of iron into the plasma, causing progressive systemic hemosiderin accumulation and organ toxicity. CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: (1) Liver: Hepatomegaly, fibrosis, micronodular cirrhosis, and markedly increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC, 20- to 200-fold increase); (2) Pancreas: Destruction of beta-islet cells resulting in secondary diabetes mellitus ('bronze diabetes'); (3) Skin: Hyperpigmentation (slate-gray or bronze) from melanin and hemosiderin deposition; (4) Joints: Degenerative arthropathy classically affecting the SECOND AND THIRD MCP JOINTS, wrists, and knees, frequently showing calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD/pseudogout) deposition with hooked chondrocalcinosis; (5) Heart: Dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy and conduction arrhythmias; (6) Pituitary / Gonads: Iron deposition in gonadotropic cells of the anterior pituitary causing secondary hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (loss of libido, erectile dysfunction, testicular atrophy). DIAGNOSTIC STRATEGY: (1) Initial screen: FASTING TRANSFERRIN SATURATION (serum iron / TIBC x 100). A transferrin saturation >= 45% (here 81%) is the most sensitive screening marker, followed by elevated serum ferritin (> 1,000 ng/mL indicates increased risk of cirrhosis); (2) CONFIRMATORY TESTING: HFE GENETIC TESTING for C282Y and H63D mutations. Liver biopsy is reserved only for patients with ferritin > 1,000 ng/mL or elevated transaminases to stage cirrhosis; (3) DEFINITIVE TREATMENT: THERAPEUTIC PHLEBOTOMY is the gold-standard disease-modifying treatment. Weekly removal of 1 unit of blood (500 mL ~ 200-250 mg elemental iron) until serum ferritin reaches 50 to 100 ng/mL, followed by maintenance phlebotomy every 2-4 months. Phlebotomy reverses hepatic fibrosis, skin pigmentation, and cardiac dysfunction, though established arthropathy and hypogonadism often fail to improve.

options.text: Administration of intramuscular testosterone replacement therapy as primary monotherapy to correct hypogonadism
options.explanation: Testosterone alone does not address systemic iron overload; unaddressed iron accumulation leads to cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and fatal cardiomyopathy; phlebotomy is the vital disease-modifying priority.

topic: Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features Treatment Modalities
stem: A 46-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of severe depressed mood, withdrawal, and bizarre beliefs that have escalated over the past 2 months. She has lost 16 pounds, sleeps less than 2 hours nightly, and spends her days rocking silently in a darkened bedroom. During the clinical interview, she speaks in a monotone whisper with prolonged latencies. She tearfully states that her intestines and stomach have completely dried up and rotted away, and that her decaying organs have contaminated the municipal water supply, causing a widespread cholera epidemic that will kill thousands of innocent children. She insists that she deserves execution to pay for her sins. Her husband confirms that she has no prior history of psychiatric illness, substance abuse, or manic episodes. Physical examination reveals an emaciated, dehydrated woman with normal vital signs, flat affect, and severe psychomotor retardation; neurological examination is completely intact. Routine laboratory evaluation, including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and urine toxicology screen, is entirely normal. Head CT without contrast reveals no acute intracranial abnormality. Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial treatment regimen for this patient?

options.text: Antidepressant monotherapy with high-dose oral escitalopram 20 mg daily

topic: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Ovulation Induction with Letrozole
stem: A 27-year-old nulligravid woman presents to the reproductive endocrinology clinic with an 18-month history of inability to conceive despite frequent, unprotected sexual intercourse. Her menstrual cycles have been irregular since menarche at age 13, currently occurring every 60 to 90 days. She also complains of persistent, severe facial acne refractory to topical retinoids and worsening dark, coarse hair growth on her chin, upper lip, chest, and lower abdomen, requiring weekly tweezing and waxing. She takes no medications. Physical examination reveals an obese woman (BMI 33.8 kg/m2). Vital signs: blood pressure 128/82 mm Hg, heart rate 72/min. Dermatologic examination reveals coarse terminal hair on the chin, upper lip, periareolar regions, and linea alba, consistent with a modified Ferriman-Gallwey score of 14 (abnormal >= 8). Velvety, hyperpigmented plaques are noted in the axillae and posterior neck, consistent with acanthosis nigricans. Pelvic examination is normal without clitoromegaly or adnexal masses. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrates bilateral enlarged ovaries (volumes 14 mL and 16 mL; normal < 10 mL) with more than 20 small, peripheral subcapsular follicles measuring 2 to 8 mm surrounding an echogenic central stroma in a classic 'string of pearls' distribution. Laboratory evaluation shows normal serum TSH, normal prolactin, and a normal morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone (110 ng/dL, ruling out non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia). Partner's semen analysis shows normal volume, concentration, and motility. Hysterosalpingography confirms bilateral tubal patency. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy to achieve ovulation and pregnancy in this patient?

options.text: Oral letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor)
options.explanation: POLYCYSTIC OVARY SYNDROME (PCOS) is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility and hyperandrogenism in reproductive-aged women. DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (ROTTERDAM 2003 / 2023 INTERNATIONAL CONSENSUS): Requires at least TWO of the following three features, after excluding mimicking disorders (congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease, Cushing syndrome, and androgen-secreting tumors): (1) OLIGO- OR ANOVULATION (irregular cycles, oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea); (2) CLINICAL AND/OR BIOCHEMICAL HYPERANDROGENISM (hirsutism, acne, male-pattern alopecia; elevated total or free testosterone); (3) POLYCYSTIC OVARIAN MORPHOLOGY ON ULTRASOUND (>= 20 follicles per ovary measuring 2-9 mm and/or ovarian volume >= 10 mL). PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Abnormal GnRH pulsatility causes excess LH relative to FSH (LH:FSH ratio > 2:1), stimulating thecal cell androgen production. Coexisting peripheral INSULIN RESISTANCE hyperstimulates ovarian thecal androgens and reduces hepatic SHBG synthesis, increasing bioavailable free testosterone. Hyperandrogenism prevents dominant follicle selection, causing follicular arrest and anovulation. MANAGEMENT OF INFERTILITY IN PCOS: (1) Lifestyle modifications (diet, exercise, 5-10% weight loss restores spontaneous ovulation in many); (2) FIRST-LINE PHARMACOLOGIC OVULATION INDUCTION: ORAL LETROZOLE (AROMATASE INHIBITOR). Landmark clinical trials, specifically the NICHD PPCOS II trial (Legro et al., NEJM 2014), demonstrated that LETROZOLE RESULTS IN SIGNIFICANTLY HIGHER CUMULATIVE LIVE BIRTH RATES (27.5% vs 19.1%) AND HIGHER OVULATION RATES compared to clomiphene citrate in women with PCOS, with shorter time to pregnancy and a lower risk of multiple gestation. Mechanism: Letrozole reversibly inhibits aromatase, blocking androgen conversion to estrogens. Reduced circulating estrogen eliminates negative hypothalamic-pituitary feedback, triggering endogenous pituitary FSH secretion that drives follicular maturation. (Clomiphene citrate, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, was historically first-line but is now second-line due to anti-estrogenic effects on the endometrium and cervical mucus). Note: For patients NOT seeking pregnancy, first-line medical therapy is combined oral contraceptives.

options.text: Oral clomiphene citrate (a selective estrogen receptor modulator)
options.explanation: While clomiphene citrate was historically first-line, the randomized PPCOS II trial demonstrated that letrozole achieves significantly higher live birth and ovulation rates with lower multiple-gestation rates in PCOS, making letrozole the undisputed first-line agent.

options.text: Metformin monotherapy at 1,500 mg daily
options.explanation: Metformin improves insulin sensitivity and metabolic parameters in PCOS, but it is substantially inferior to letrozole for inducing ovulation and achieving live birth and is not recommended as first-line monotherapy for fertility.

options.text: Exogenous gonadotropin therapy (intramuscular human menopausal gonadotropins / recombinant FSH)
options.explanation: Injectable gonadotropins are second-line therapy for patients who fail oral ovulation induction with letrozole; they carry high risks of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) and high-order multiple gestations.

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pills containing ethinyl estradiol and drospirenone
options.explanation: Combined oral contraceptives are first-line for regulating menses and suppressing hyperandrogenism in women NOT desiring pregnancy; they suppress ovulation and prevent conception, which directly conflicts with this patient's fertility goals.

subject: Medicine
topic: Delirium vs Dementia Differentiation and Non-Pharmacological Management
stem: An 81-year-old man who was hospitalized 48 hours ago for right lower lobe community-acquired pneumonia treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin becomes acutely agitated, combative, and confused at 2:30 AM. He attempts to climb out of his hospital bed, pulls at his peripheral intravenous cannula, and screams that large black spiders are crawling across the ceiling tiles and that the night nurse is an imposter trying to poison him. His daughter, who is staying at the bedside, is extremely distressed; she reports that prior to this acute illness, he lived independently in his own home, drove daily, managed his financial investments, and had completely normal cognitive memory and functional independence. Vital signs: temperature 38.0 C (100.4 F), blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg, heart rate 94/min, respirations 20/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. Physical examination reveals an ill-appearing, restless man. Neurological examination reveals that his level of consciousness fluctuates from hyperalert agitation to drowsy lethargy. He cannot maintain focus, is unable to spell 'WORLD' backward or recite the days of the week in reverse order, and speaks in disjointed, fragmented sentences. Cranial nerves are intact, and there are no focal motor deficits, neck stiffness, or asterixis. Serum sodium is 135 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, BUN 24 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Immediate application of four-point soft wrist and ankle restraints to prevent falls and catheter dislodgement
options.explanation: Physical restraints are strictly contraindicated as first-line management; they dramatically intensify panic and combative agitation, prolong delirium duration, and cause severe trauma and strangulation.

options.text: Diagnosis of acute hyperactive delirium precipitated by systemic infection, managed with multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions (verbal reorientation, family presence, circadian lighting) and avoidance of physical restraints
options.explanation: DELIRIUM VS DEMENTIA DIFFERENTIATION: (1) DELIRIUM is an ACUTE (hours to days), FLUCTUATING disturbance in ATTENTION (reduced ability to direct, focus, sustain, and shift attention) and AWARENESS (reduced orientation to the environment), accompanied by cognitive change (memory deficit, perceptual disturbances such as visual hallucinations/delusions) triggered by an underlying medical condition, substance intoxication/withdrawal, or medication side effect. (2) DEMENTIA (MAJOR NEUROCOGNITIVE DISORDER) is an INSIDIOUS (months to years), PROGRESSIVE decline in cognitive domains with PRESERVED ALERTNESS AND ATTENTION until advanced stages. This patient's abrupt onset, acute fluctuation in alertness, visual hallucinations, and baseline normal functional independence definitively establish DELIRIUM precipitated by pneumonia. NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT (FIRST-LINE): Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP) and clinical practice guidelines emphasize MULTICOMPONENT NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL INTERVENTIONS as the foundation of delirium management: (a) Frequent verbal reorientation and presence of familiar family members; (b) Maintaining sleep-wake hygiene (daytime natural light and mobilization, quiet and dark environment at night); (c) Providing sensory aids (glasses, hearing aids); (d) Minimizing invasive tethers (early removal of urinary catheters and unnecessary IV lines); (e) AVOIDANCE OF PHYSICAL RESTRAINTS: Physical restraints directly worsen agitation, increase delirium duration, and cause severe asphyxiation or injury. PHARMACOTHERAPY (ANTIPSYCHOTICS): Antipsychotics (e.g., low-dose haloperidol or quetiapine) DO NOT PREVENT OR SHORTEN DELIRIUM DURATION and carry risks of QTc prolongation, extrapyramidal symptoms, and increased mortality. They are strictly reserved as a last resort for severe agitation that poses an immediate, serious physical danger to the patient or staff.

options.text: Administration of high-dose intravenous lorazepam 2 mg bolus for acute sedation
options.explanation: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) directly worsen and prolong delirium, increase the risk of paradoxical disinhibition, respiratory depression, and falls, and are strictly contraindicated except in alcohol or sedative withdrawal.

options.text: Initiation of daily oral donepezil 5 mg for newly diagnosed Alzheimer disease
options.explanation: Donepezil is a cholinesterase inhibitor for chronic progressive Alzheimer dementia; initiating it for acute infection-induced delirium has zero efficacy, causes cholinergic gastrointestinal toxicity, and delays necessary delirium interventions.

options.text: Immediate continuous intravenous haloperidol infusion to achieve rapid neuroleptic calming
options.explanation: Continuous IV haloperidol is associated with severe QTc prolongation, torsades de pointes, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome; antipsychotics should never be given as continuous infusions or routine delirium therapy.

subject: Surgery
topic: Unstable Open-Book Pelvic Fracture Resuscitation and Pelvic Binder Application
stem: A 36-year-old construction worker is brought by emergency medical services to the level 1 trauma center after falling 25 feet from a scaffold onto concrete. On arrival, he is pale, cool, diaphoretic, and groaning with severe lower abdominal and pelvic pain. Primary survey reveals an intact airway with bilateral clear breath sounds and no chest wall instability. Vital signs: blood pressure 76/44 mm Hg, heart rate 138/min, respirations 26/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on non-rebreather mask. Physical examination reveals exquisite tenderness to palpation over the anterior pelvis; gentle manual compression of both anterior superior iliac spines demonstrates abnormal lateral displacement and gross pelvic instability with palpable crepitus. Extensive perineal and scrotal ecchymosis is present, and a small drop of blood is visualized at the urethral meatus. Abdominal FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) examination reveals free fluid in the rectovesical pouch without fluid in the hepatorenal or splenorenal recesses. A portable anteroposterior pelvic radiograph obtained in the trauma bay demonstrates a 4.5-cm diastasis of the pubic symphysis with disruption of the right sacroiliac joint, consistent with an anteroposterior compression (APC) type III 'open-book' pelvic fracture. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the emergency management of this patient?

options.text: Immediate transfer to the operating room for emergent exploratory laparotomy and iliac vessel surgical clamping
options.explanation: Pelvic venous hemorrhage cannot be controlled by laparotomy; opening the retroperitoneum releases the precarious tamponade and accelerates fatal exsanguination; pelvic binding followed by preperitoneal packing or angiography is standard.

options.text: Application of a pelvic binder centered high over the iliac crests combined with rapid infusion of 3 liters of warm 0.9% normal saline
options.explanation: Centering a binder over the iliac crests is anatomically incorrect and displaces fractures; furthermore, aggressive crystalloid hemodilution disrupts coagulation and worsens mortality compared to balanced 1:1:1 blood transfusion.

options.text: Emergent application of a circumferential pelvic compression device (pelvic binder) centered precisely over the greater trochanters, combined with activation of the massive transfusion protocol (1:1:1 pRBCs, FFP, and platelets)
options.explanation: UNSTABLE 'OPEN-BOOK' PELVIC FRACTURE RESUSCITATION: MECHANISM AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Severe anteroposterior compression (APC II/III) disruptions tear the anterior pubic symphysis and posterior sacroiliac ligaments, allowing the hemipelvis to rotate externally ('open-book'). This dramatically INCREASES THE INTRAPELVIC VOLUME, creating an open space that abolishes the normal tamponade effect. Hemorrhage in pelvic fractures originates primarily from: (1) LOW-PRESSURE RETROPERITONEAL AND PRESACRAL VENOUS PLEXUSES (85-90% of bleeding); (2) Bleeding from cancellous fractured bone surfaces; (3) Arterial injury (internal iliac branches: superior gluteal, internal pudendal, lateral sacral, 10-15% of bleeding). Life-threatening exsanguination occurs within minutes. IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY STABILIZATION: (1) PELVIC CIRCUMFERENTIAL COMPRESSION (PELVIC BINDER): Applying a commercial non-invasive pelvic binder (or folded bedsheet) IMMEDIATELY reduces pelvic volume, closes the diastasis, and restores retroperitoneal tissue pressure to tamponade venous bleeding and stop fractured bone bleeding. CRITICAL ANATOMIC PLACEMENT: The pelvic binder MUST BE CENTERED OVER THE GREATER TROCHANTERS (at the level of the pubic symphysis). Placing it higher over the iliac crests is ineffective and can actually worsen fracture displacement; (2) DAMAGE CONTROL RESUSCITATION: Immediate activation of the MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL using balanced 1:1:1 ratios of packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets; avoid large crystalloid infusions that disrupt clot formation. (3) NEXT STEPS BASED ON HEMODYNAMIC RESPONSE: If hemodynamic instability persists despite pelvic binding and blood resuscitation: (a) If FAST is positive for intraperitoneal hemorrhage -> Emergent laparotomy and preperitoneal pelvic packing; (b) If instability persists from retroperitoneal arterial hemorrhage -> Emergent pelvic angiography and transcatheter arterial embolization.

options.explanation: Blood at the urethral meatus and scrotal ecchymosis indicate suspected urethral disruption; blind Foley catheterization is contraindicated until a retrograde urethrogram rules out urethral transection.

subject: Medicine
topic: Infective Endocarditis Indications for Urgent Valve Replacement Surgery
stem: A 54-year-old man with a known history of a congenitally bicuspid aortic valve is hospitalized for native valve infective endocarditis caused by penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus mitis (viridans group streptococci). He has completed 6 days of targeted intravenous ceftriaxone therapy. On hospital day 7, he develops sudden-onset severe shortness of breath, orthopnea, and anxiety. Vital signs: blood pressure 104/42 mm Hg (wide pulse pressure), heart rate 116/min and regular, respirations 28/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on 4 L/min nasal cannula. Cardiovascular examination reveals an early diastolic, decrescendo high-pitched murmur heard best along the left sternal border with the patient leaning forward, along with an S3 gallop and soft S1. Bilateral pulmonary examination reveals diffuse fine end-inspiratory crackles extending through the mid-lung fields bilaterally. Peripheral pulses are bounding (water-hammer pulses). Urgent transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography reveals acute severe aortic regurgitation with holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta, premature closure of the mitral valve in late diastole, and a 14-mm mobile, pedunculated vegetation on the right coronary cusp of the aortic valve. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 58% with normal cavity dimensions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.text: Completion of a 4-week course of intravenous ceftriaxone before considering elective outpatient valve replacement
options.explanation: Waiting to complete a 4-week antibiotic course in the setting of acute severe aortic regurgitation and pulmonary edema leads to irreversible cardiogenic shock and death; urgent surgery is mandatory.

options.text: Administration of intravenous loop diuretics and initiation of oral afterload reduction with an ACE inhibitor, avoiding surgical intervention
options.explanation: Medical management with vasodilators and diuretics cannot reverse structural valve destruction; while temporizing, it is entirely insufficient, and delaying surgery carries high operative and in-hospital mortality.

options.text: Urgent transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) to avoid the morbidity of open sternotomy
options.explanation: TAVR is contraindicated in active infective endocarditis because the prosthetic valve cannot anchor securely into destroyed, infected annular tissue, risks fatal paravalvular leak, and spreads persistent infection.

options.text: Urgent surgical aortic valve replacement combined with continuation of targeted intravenous bactericidal antibiotic therapy
options.explanation: INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS (IE) SURGICAL INDICATIONS: While medical antimicrobial therapy cures many uncomplicated native valve IE cases, approximately 50% of patients develop complications requiring early surgical valve replacement. INDICATIONS FOR EARLY / URGENT SURGICAL INTERVENTION (AHA/ACC and ESC Guidelines): (1) HEART FAILURE / HEMODYNAMIC COMPROMISE (MOST COMMON AND DECISIVE INDICATION): Acute severe aortic or mitral regurgitation resulting in pulmonary edema, refractory cardiogenic shock, or echocardiographic signs of elevated LV end-diastolic pressure (such as PREMATURE CLOSURE OF THE MITRAL VALVE). Acute severe aortic regurgitation poorly accommodates large regurgitant volumes because the non-compliant, normal-sized left ventricle experiences precipitous rises in LVEDP, rapidly exceeding left atrial pressure and closing the mitral valve prematurely before ventricular systole. Medical management alone carries > 75% in-hospital mortality; urgent surgical valve replacement is Class I indicated regardless of antibiotic duration; (2) UNCONTROLLED LOCAL INFECTION: Persistent bacteremia or unrelenting fever despite > 7-10 days of targeted bactericidal antibiotic therapy, perivalvular extension (aortic root abscess, fistula, pseudoaneurysm, or new heart block); (3) PREVENTION OF RECURRENT EMBOLISM: Large, persistent mobile vegetations (> 10 mm in length), especially on the aortic or mitral valve and particularly following an embolic event or accompanied by mobile components. This patient has acute severe aortic regurgitation causing acute left heart failure, pulmonary edema, premature mitral valve closure, and a 14-mm vegetation—an absolute, life-saving indication for urgent surgical valve replacement.

options.text: Switching intravenous ceftriaxone to intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin, and rifampin triple therapy
options.explanation: The clinical deterioration is due to mechanical acute valve destruction and hemodynamic failure, not antibiotic resistance (viridans streptococci is penicillin-susceptible); changing antimicrobials does not fix structural valve rupture.

topic: Secondary Syphilis Clinical Manifestations and Benzathine Penicillin G Treatment
stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 2-week history of a widespread rash, fatigue, low-grade fevers, and generalized muscle aches. He recalls having a solitary, painless ulcer on the shaft of his penis approximately 6 weeks ago that resolved spontaneously over 3 weeks without medical evaluation or treatment. He is sexually active with two female partners and occasionally uses condoms. Vital signs: temperature 37.8 C (100.0 F), blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, heart rate 74/min, and respirations 14/min. Physical examination reveals diffuse, symmetrical, non-pruritic, reddish-brown macules and papules (1 to 5 mm) distributed over his trunk and extremities, with prominent involvement of the bilateral palmar surfaces of his hands and plantar surfaces of his feet. Examination of the perianal area demonstrates several moist, broad-based, flat, grayish-white plaque-like vegetations in the gluteal cleft. Examination of the oral cavity reveals shallow, painless mucosal erosions with an erythematous border on the inner lower lip. Non-tender, rubbery lymphadenopathy is palpable in the posterior cervical, axillary, epitrochlear, and inguinal chains. Neurological examination is completely normal. Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titer is markedly positive at 1:128, and a confirmatory Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TP-PA) assay is reactive. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.text: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 28 consecutive days
options.explanation: Doxycycline for 14 days is an alternative for penicillin-allergic non-pregnant patients; however, parenteral benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose is the preferred first-line therapy with superior cure rates.

options.text: Intramuscular administration of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks
options.explanation: Three weekly doses of benzathine penicillin G are indicated for late latent syphilis (> 1 year duration), tertiary syphilis, or syphilis of unknown duration; early secondary syphilis requires only a single dose.

options.text: Continuous intravenous infusion of aqueous crystalline penicillin G 24 million units daily for 14 days
options.explanation: Intravenous crystalline penicillin G is the treatment of choice for neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, or otosyphilis; in the absence of neurological signs, early secondary syphilis is treated with a single IM injection.

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 10 days
options.explanation: Oral aminopenicillins have inadequate pharmacokinetic profiles and do not achieve prolonged treponemicidal levels; benzathine penicillin G depot injection is mandatory to clear T. pallidum.

options.text: Intramuscular administration of a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units
options.explanation: SECONDARY SYPHILIS: Treponema pallidum is a microaerophilic spirochete that causes syphilis. STAGES AND NATURAL HISTORY: (1) PRIMARY SYPHILIS: Characterized by a painless, indurated ulcer (chancre) at the site of inoculation accompanied by non-tender regional lymphadenopathy, healing spontaneously in 3-6 weeks; (2) SECONDARY SYPHILIS: Occurs 4 to 10 weeks after primary infection as spirochetes disseminate hematogenously. CLINICAL HALLMARKS: (a) RASH: Diffuse, symmetrical maculopapular or papulosquamous rash classically involving the PALMS AND SOLES (copper-penny lesions); (b) CONDYLOMATA LATA: Highly infectious, moist, flat, broad-based, cauliflower-like plaques in intertriginous and genital areas; (c) MUCOUS PATCHES: Painless shallow oral mucosal erosions; (d) GENERALIZED LYMPHADENOPATHY: Characteristically involving the EPITROCHLEAR NODES (highly suggestive of syphilis); (e) Constitutional symptoms: Low-grade fever, malaise, pharyngitis, patchy 'moth-eaten' alopecia; (3) LATENT SYPHILIS: Asymptomatic period (early latent < 1 year; late latent > 1 year); (4) TERTIARY SYPHILIS: Gummas, cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis, aortic aneurysm), and neurosyphilis. TREATMENT GUIDELINES (CDC 2021 STI Guidelines): (a) EARLY SYPHILIS (PRIMARY, SECONDARY, AND EARLY LATENT < 1 YEAR): A SINGLE INTRAMUSCULAR DOSE OF BENZATHINE PENICILLIN G 2.4 MILLION UNITS. (Note: Penicillin G benzathine is long-acting depot; aqueous or procaine formulations cannot be substituted). In non-pregnant penicillin-allergic patients, oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days is an alternative; (b) LATE LATENT (> 1 YEAR OR UNKNOWN DURATION): Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM ONCE WEEKLY FOR 3 CONSECUTIVE WEEKS (total 7.2 million units); (c) NEUROSYPHILIS: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18-24 million units/day IV for 10-14 days. Following treatment, patients should be warned about the JARISCH-HERXHEIMER REACTION (acute fever, chills, tachycardia, and exacerbation of rash occurring within 24 hours due to massive spirochetal lysis releasing endotoxin-like pyrogens), which is managed supportively with antipyretics.
